```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(easyNIS)
```

`nis_comorbidity()` uses the optional `medicalcoder` package to apply its
AHRQ Elixhauser ICD-10-CM mapping. easyNIS does not distribute clinical code
lists. This computation is experimental and its assumptions need scientific
review.

## Score a DuckDB cohort

Keep `KEY_NIS` and, for pooled years, `YEAR` with the diagnosis columns.
The function scores batches of up to 25,000 discharges, reading only the
keys, diagnoses and available POA fields into the scoring workflow. The
result remains a DuckDB query with the original columns and the added
indicators. Select the columns you need before collecting.

The example assigns stable keys to the invented fixture. NIS files already
include `KEY_NIS`.

```{r comorbidity, eval=rlang::is_installed("medicalcoder", version = "0.10.0")}
discharges <- nis_open(nis_example(years = 2019)) |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 18) |>
  dplyr::mutate(KEY_NIS = dplyr::row_number()) |>
  dplyr::compute()
scored <- nis_comorbidity(discharges)
scored |>
  dplyr::select(AGE, cmrb_n, cmrb_any, cmrb_mortality_index) |>
  head() |>
  dplyr::collect()
```

The added columns report the number of flagged conditions and whether any
were flagged. Values are computed from invented codes. Rows without usable
ICD-10 codes have missing results rather than “no comorbidity.”

Scores are computed when you call `nis_comorbidity()` and kept in a temporary
table for the input connection. DuckDB reads the original query again when
you use its output, so score a stable cohort with unique, non-missing keys.
Collected data frames are also supported and keep their original row order.

## Add scores after design construction

If an analysis uses `nis_design()`, keep diagnosis columns in the design and
pass the design to `nis_comorbidity()`. This preserves the design object.

```{r design, eval=rlang::is_installed("medicalcoder", version = "0.10.0")}
nis <- nis_open(nis_example(years = 2019)) |>
  nis_flag_dx(heart_failure = "I50")
design <- nis_design(
  nis,
  cohort = heart_failure,
  keep = c(AGE, dplyr::starts_with("I10_DX"), dplyr::starts_with("DXPOA"))
)
scored_design <- nis_comorbidity(design)
head(scored_design$variables[c("AGE", "cmrb_n", "cmrb_any")])
```

The survey design fields remain the same while the analysis variables gain
comorbidity indicators.

## Present on admission

AHRQ assigns 18 of its 38 refined Elixhauser measures using POA for
nonexempt secondary diagnoses. For those diagnoses, `Y` and `W` qualify.
NIS files lack POA indicators. AHRQ leaves those 18 measures missing when
POA inputs are unavailable and requires all 38 to calculate its indices.
Beginning in 2019, the NIS Diagnosis and
Procedure Groups file includes the available HCUP-derived measures.
[AHRQ User Guide](https://hcup-us.ahrq.gov/toolssoftware/comorbidityicd10/CMR-User-Guide-v2024-1.pdf),
[HCUP POA availability](https://hcup-us.ahrq.gov/db/vars/sedddistnote.jsp?var=cmr_aaa),
[2019 NIS introduction](https://hcup-us.ahrq.gov/db/nation/nis/NIS_Introduction_2019.jsp).

`nis_comorbidity()` retains its experimental assumption that a diagnosis
was present on admission when its entire `DXPOAn` field is absent. The
warning identifies the affected slots. This assumption can count conditions
that arose during the stay and alter the mortality and readmission scores.
When a matching field is present, `Y` and `W` count as POA, `N` and `U`
do not, and other values are unknown. In pooled data, a missing value in an
existing POA column remains unknown. `medicalcoder` supplies the exempt-code
mapping, which is shared across AHRQ releases in that package and is applied
without looking up the fiscal year for each discharge.

Pre-October 2015 ICD-9 records receive missing results. Older Stata-derived
`ynel*` and `elixsum` fields use different definitions and versions.

## Charlson in NIS studies

Charlson serves different purposes across studies. The national inpatient
norms study used Quan's ICD-10 algorithms to describe comorbidity burden by
demographic groups. The NIS hepatitis C pregnancy study used the
Charlson–Deyo score as an adjustment covariate, grouping it into 0, 1–2,
and above 2.
[National norms study](https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glac087),
[hepatitis C pregnancy study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10362466/).

easyNIS defers a Charlson option until it can specify and verify the mapping,
weights, diagnosis inclusion, and POA assumptions for a named variant.
`medicalcoder` supplies Quan 2005 and 2011 variants, with distinct weights
and explicit POA and principal-diagnosis inputs. The `comorbidity` package
offers a Quan ICD-10 map with separately selectable original or revised
weights and a severity hierarchy. For a replication, choose these inputs
using the study's methods.
[`medicalcoder` Charlson vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/medicalcoder/vignettes/charlson.html),
[`comorbidity` manual](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/comorbidity/comorbidity.pdf).

See [`nis_comorbidity()`](../reference/nis_comorbidity.html) and
[Data notes by year](year-notes.html).
